newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks concrete results at Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks concrete results at Mideast summit.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton hoped on Wednesday to persuade the leaders of Israel and the Palestinians to translate their new civility into concrete steps to reinvigorate the Middle East peace process.

But there apparently were no guarantees of tangible results at the emergency summit that on Tuesday saw Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat meet alone with aides for three hours.
It was only the second face-to-face meeting between the two leaders, who previously have displayed barely disguised disdain for each other.
"Working-level officials continued discussions on through the night and are continuing as we speak. The work goes on," a U.S. official told Reuters early on Wednesday.
Asked if there was any substantive progress to point to, the official said: "The meetings themselves. The fact that the talks are continuing."
"We are going to continue to stay out of a discussion of the substance until that is appropriate, and we're not there yet," said the official, who asked not to be identified.

Clinton called the summit in a bid to prevent a collapse of the peace process following gun battles and clashes that took the lives of 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week.
He was to meet Netanyahu, Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein in the White House Blue Room at 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT), and that session was to be followed by a working lunch.

The principals were scheduled to make public statements summarizing their two days of talks at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) -- a sign that they expected to have something to announce -- but few White House insiders expected the news conference to start at anything close to the scheduled time.
Asked if there were any plans for Netanyahu and Arafat to meet alone again on Wednesday, the U.S. official said, "I'm not aware of any." But he hastened to add that such a meeting was possible.

On the only concrete point divulged by officials about Tuesday's talks, Israel said it stood firm against U.S. pressure to set a date to complete a long-delayed pullback of troops from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Palestinians view Hebron, the last and most sensitive of the cities slated for handover under an agreement sealed at the White House one year ago, as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he reluctantly inherited when he came to power at the head of a hardline government in June.
"In traditional Middle East diplomacy, the negotiators will work all night long and then sleep through the closing ceremonies," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, only half in jest.

Last week's Middle East fighting was sparked by Israel's decision to open another entrance to a tourist tunnel alongside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, holy to Moslems and Jews. But it also reflected Arab frustrations at what they consider Israel's slow pace in pursuing peace accords.

Palestinians demand that Israel close the tunnel, carry out the pullback from Hebron -- home to 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews -- and ease a closure barring Palestinians from jobs in Gaza and the West Bank.

Netanyahu has toughened his stance since the violence erupted, accusing Arafat of ordering his police force to fire at Israelis the guns the peace deal provided. But a new opinion poll on Tuesday showed 80 percent of Israelis want him to press ahead with peace moves.
